title: Not Louder, Better Designed: The Last Metre of Public Engagement
subtitle: Public engagement rarely fails for lack of information. It fails in the last metre. Policy is written in documents; behaviour happens on site — and the space between the two is where the work actually is. When a programme underdelivers, the instinct is to turn up the volume: more reminders, more channels, more urgency. It rarely works, because the audience was never short of a message. They were short of a moment — the second at which taking part becomes the easiest thing available. That is a design problem rather than a communications one, and — unlike volume — it can be measured. The numbers below describe the market that surrounds that moment: what Hong Kong already spends, how much activity it already runs, and what the physical layer of public engagement is worth.

title: Strategic Nudges: Small Prompts, Measurable Behaviour
subtitle: The best nudge is not a louder message — it is a better-designed choice at the moment of decision. That one line separates two entirely different ways of changing behaviour. The loud way keeps adding pressure: more reminders, more urgency, more noise, all of it trying to change what people want. The designed way changes the decision itself — the form placed in their hand, the default already ticked, the sign standing exactly where they hesitate, the object given at the second it is needed. Nothing is demanded of anyone's willpower, and nothing has to be taken away from the experience. The right choice simply becomes easier to make than to avoid. Which is why the numbers on this page are not a story about persuasion. They are a story about design.
